title: Technology and Analytics — Automating a Close Bottleneck with RPA, and Controlling the Bot
scenario: Northstar Services runs its field-service dispatch on one system and its general ledger on another, with no interface between them. Every month six analysts each spend 20 hours re-keying job, labor, and materials data from the dispatch system into the general ledger so the close can be completed. Their fully burdened cost is $50 per hour. A vendor proposes a robotic process automation bot that would read the dispatch extract and post the entries automatically, eliminating 75% of those hours. The bot costs $60,000 to build in the first year plus a $12,000 annual license and maintenance fee. Answer each requirement in complete sentences and show your computations.

requirements.prompt: Requirement 1 — Compute the annual cost of the manual effort, the annual savings the bot would deliver, the net cash effect in the first year, the steady-state annual net benefit, and the payback period on the build cost. State whether Northstar should approve the project.

noneOf: the first year is cash positive

requirements.modelAnswer: Six analysts at 20 hours each consume 120 hours a month, which at $50 an hour is $6,000 monthly and $72,000 a year. Eliminating 75% of that effort saves $54,000 annually. In the first year Northstar also pays the $60,000 build and the $12,000 license, so the net is negative in the first year by $18,000. From the second year forward only the $12,000 fee recurs, leaving a steady-state net benefit of $42,000 a year, and the build cost divided by that benefit gives a payback of roughly 1.4 years, or about 17 months. Northstar should approve the project, because a $60,000 investment that returns $42,000 a year indefinitely clears any reasonable hurdle, and the reclaimed analyst hours can be redirected to review work that shortens the close.

requirements.prompt: Requirement 2 — Explain why the re-keying exists at all and whether RPA or a true system interface is the better long-run answer. Then identify the information-technology general controls Northstar must put around the bot before it is allowed to post journal entries.

anyOf: a true interface is the better long-run answer
an interface is the durable fix
integration is the better long-term solution
the permanent answer is an interface
the bot must have its own credentials
segregation of duties applies to the bot
noneOf: the bot needs no access controls

requirements.modelAnswer: The re-keying exists because dispatch and the general ledger were bought separately and no interface ever connected them, so people are acting as the missing data flow. Robotic process automation solves the symptom by driving the same screens a person would, which makes it fast to deploy but brittle: a field moves or a screen changes and the bot silently fails. A true interface is the better long-run answer, because passing structured data between the systems removes the manual step for good, and the bot should be treated as a bridge that buys time. Before it posts anything, the bot must have its own credentials in a named service account carrying least-privilege rights, so its activity is distinguishable from a human's. Change management must require testing and independent approval of every bot revision, and its postings need logging plus a monthly exception review by the controller.
